analysis.one_liner: Extends health coverage for new mothers and funds programs to prevent maternal deaths, paid for by higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: A maternal mortality bill with 64 House cosponsors — all Democrats — never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The MOMMA's Act would extend Medicaid and CHIP coverage for new mothers from 60 days after childbirth to a full year, require those programs to cover dental care during and after pregnancy, and extend WIC nutrition benefits for postpartum women to two years. It funds CDC data collection on maternal deaths, grants to state teams that improve childbirth safety, and training for doctors on implicit bias, with CMS guidance so states can cover doula services. To pay for it, the bill roughly doubles the federal cigarette tax (about $1 more per pack) and raises taxes on other tobacco products to match. It sat in three House committees for the entire two-year Congress and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income pregnant and postpartum women, most of them on Medicaid: they would keep coverage for a full year after birth instead of losing it at 60 days — a window that matters, because the bill's own findings note nearly half of maternal deaths occur after delivery. It also benefits families relying on WIC, patients served by doulas and better-trained providers, and states, which would receive a 100% federal match for the cost of the extended postpartum coverage during the first five years.

how_it_helps.text: Extends Medicaid and CHIP postpartum coverage from 60 days to one full year after pregnancy ends, with the federal government paying 100% of the cost of the extended coverage for the first five years and 90% thereafter.
Requires Medicaid and CHIP to cover preventive, diagnostic, periodontal, and restorative dental care for pregnant and postpartum women.
Extends WIC nutrition eligibility for postpartum women from one year to two years.

Directs the CDC to provide technical assistance on standardizing maternal death reporting, funds a national Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health grant program ($10 million a year) and state perinatal quality collaboratives ($14 million a year), and creates regional centers to train health professionals on implicit bias and culturally competent care.
Directs CMS to issue guidance on Medicaid coverage and payment for doula services, which evidence cited in the bill links to fewer birth complications and lower costs.

Pays for the package by raising the federal cigarette tax from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand (about $1 more per pack), raising taxes on cigars, pipe tobacco, smokeless products, and roll-your-own tobacco to match, taxing FDA-designated nicotine products at cigarette-equivalent rates, and indexing all tobacco taxes to inflation.
Bars states from making Medicaid or CHIP eligibility for pregnant women more restrictive for five years, so the expansion cannot be quietly rolled back.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco users — disproportionately lower-income adults — who would pay roughly $1 more per pack of cigarettes and comparable increases on other tobacco products. State Medicaid programs would eventually share the cost of the extended coverage once the federal match drops to 90%, and states must also meet minimum dental coverage standards for pregnant women.

drawbacks.text: The tobacco tax is regressive: it takes a larger share of income from lower-income smokers, many of whom are the same population the expanded coverage aims to help.
The CDC's data-reporting assistance applies only to 'States that elect to report,' so standardized maternal death data would remain voluntary in the bill's core provision.
The program authorizations are modest — $5 to $14 million a year each — relative to a crisis the bill itself describes as roughly 700 deaths and 70,000 near-fatal complications annually.
States must cover a minimum dental package for pregnant and postpartum women and, after the enhanced federal match expires, would shoulder most of the ongoing cost of the extended coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage extension addresses the bill's most concrete, documented gap: Medicaid pregnancy coverage lapses at 60 days postpartum even though 21% of maternal deaths occur between one and six weeks after birth and another 12% later in the postpartum year. A full year of coverage, plus dental care and nutrition support, plausibly saves lives at a cost of a modest per-pack tobacco tax. The main fairness problem is that the tax falls hardest on low-income smokers; the main design weakness is that the data-reporting core is voluntary for states. On balance, the benefits to new mothers outweigh the costs, but the bill would have been stronger with a mandatory reporting requirement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to a health subcommittee in May 2021, and it sat there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Robin Kelly of Illinois introduced the MOMMA's Act on May 20, 2021, with 25 original cosponsors.
The bill attracted 64 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat; no Republican signed on.
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor committees, splitting its Medicaid, tobacco-tax, and training provisions across three committees.
On May 21, 2021, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no further action was ever recorded.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill ever receiving a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and retailers kept the existing lower federal tax rates, since the tax increase never took effect. The roughly 700 women who die from pregnancy complications each year — disproportionately Black women — and the low-income mothers who would have gained a year of coverage got nothing. The bill's 65 House supporters never even got a vote on the merits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and no one else

for.name: 64 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, growing support to 64 members within the first session.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration, even though its tobacco-tax funding provisions fell squarely in his committee's jurisdiction.

against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee

sides.party_line_note: All 64 cosponsors were Democrats and the sole sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and no vote was ever held, so no Republican ever had to take a recorded position on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would have roughly doubled the federal cigarette excise tax — about $1 more per pack — and raised taxes on cigars, pipe, smokeless, and roll-your-own tobacco to the same per-use levels, with automatic inflation increases thereafter. The industry's interest in the bill ran against the public health goal: avoiding the tax meant keeping prices lower for a product the bill links to maternal and infant harm.

industries.industry: Medicaid managed-care insurers and hospitals that deliver maternity care
industries.note: Extending postpartum Medicaid and CHIP coverage to one year would have meant a year of paid care for every pregnancy Medicaid covers, with the federal government picking up 100% of the extension cost for the first five years. The industry's gain runs alongside new mothers' interest in continuous care.

industries.industry: Doulas and the maternity care workforce
industries.note: The bill would have created federal guidance for Medicaid doula coverage and funded training centers at health professional schools, opening a new payment stream for community birth workers and strengthening provider training.
